To blabber means to talk too much — in a way that is pointless, rambling, or foolish — OR to carelessly reveal information (secrets, private details) that was supposed to stay quiet.

These two uses are connected by the same underlying idea: words coming out without enough thought or control.

1. Talking too much, uselessly

When someone blabbers, they go on and on, often saying nothing meaningful or worth listening to. The speech feels like noise — excessive, repetitive, without real substance.

"Stop blabbering and get to the point."
"He blabbered for twenty minutes without saying anything useful."
"She kept blabbering about her day while everyone around her was trying to work."

The listener is typically bored, annoyed, or simply not interested. The talker seems unaware — or doesn't care — that they're wasting everyone's time.

2. Revealing secrets or private information carelessly

Here, blabber means to let something slip — to tell people things you shouldn't. The carelessness is key. The person who blabbers a secret usually doesn't do it with planned malice; they simply can't keep their mouth shut.

"Don't blabber our plans to anyone before we're ready."
"She blabbered everything to the press the moment she left the meeting."
"I told him in confidence, and he blabbered it to the whole office."

Blabber is never neutral. It always carries a negative or mocking tone. When you describe someone as blabbering, you are being critical — you are dismissing their words as worthless, excessive, or irresponsible.

It also implies the person talking has poor self-control or poor judgment. A blabberer speaks when they should be quiet, talks more than the situation calls for, and often causes harm or irritation by doing so.

You'll hear this word used for:

  • Gossips who can't keep private information to themselves
  • People who ramble in conversations, meetings, or presentations
  • Children who excitedly reveal a surprise someone planned
  • Nervous talkers who fill silence with meaningless chatter
  • Anyone who talks more than they think
How blabber differs from similar words

A few words sit in the same neighbourhood, but each has its own shade:

  • Talk — completely neutral. No judgment at all.
  • Chat — friendly, light, informal. A warm word.
  • Babble — talking fast and unclearly, almost incomprehensibly. Think of a baby babbling. The focus is on how it sounds — garbled and hard to follow.
  • Ramble — wandering off-topic, losing the thread. A rambler drifts. The focus is on structure (or the lack of it).
  • Gossip — spreading stories and rumours about other people. The focus is on content — it's about other people's business.
  • Blabber — the focus is on excess and thoughtlessness. Too many words, too little care. Can be about anything — your own life, others' secrets, nothing in particular.
A quick way to remember it

Think of the word as sounding like what it means — it even sounds like lots of loose, bubbling words tumbling out uncontrollably: blab-blab-blab. When someone is blabbering, that's essentially what's happening — their mouth is running ahead of their mind.

To blabber is to talk excessively and thoughtlessly — either filling the air with pointless chatter, or carelessly letting out things that should have stayed unsaid. The word always signals that someone is using too many words with too little wisdom.
